summary:
After the Mission is an interactive website that treats finished space missions as case files. Visitors can browse 14 NASA missions, including ALSEP, Surveyor 3, Ingenuity, Cassini, Kepler and InSight. Each mission has real imagery, a "full case file" that follows our method (Mission Records → Evidence → Analysis → Findings), and a direct link to its official NASA page. An afterlife timeline shows how many years each mission's data and hardware have stayed useful since it ended. The site also has search, filters by Moon, Mars, Planets and Telescopes, and a "Solve the case" quiz.

It addresses the challenge by showing what happens to space technology after its mission ends. Some missions keep their science alive through archived data, like ALSEP. Others leave physical evidence, like Surveyor 3, whose parts Apollo 12 astronauts brought back to Earth. Others leave flight data that guides future designs, like Ingenuity.

This matters because the end of a mission is not the end of its scientific value. By making this evidence easy to explore, the site helps students, researchers and the public see the lasting impact of space exploration.

Team THE BIG BANG: Modi Aldossari and Jana Aldawas.
details:
What it does and how it works
After the Mission is a website that turns finished space missions into case files. It lists 14 NASA missions, from the Apollo-era ALSEP and Surveyor 3 to Ingenuity, Cassini, Kepler, InSight and Dawn. Each mission card shows an image, when the mission ended, what it left behind, and how researchers use it today. Visitors can:

  • Filter missions by Moon, Mars, Planets or Telescopes, or search by name.
  • Open a full case file that follows our method: Mission Records → Evidence → Analysis → Findings, ending with a verdict.
  • Tap a card to go straight to the mission's official NASA page.
  • View an afterlife timeline showing how long each mission's data and hardware have stayed useful since it ended.
  • Take a short "Solve the case" quiz.

Benefits
It gives students, teachers, researchers and the public one place to see that missions keep producing value after they end. Because every card links to NASA's own pages and archives, it also points people to trusted sources.

Intended impact
We want people to see that the end of a mission is not the end of its scientific value, and to encourage preserving and reusing mission data and hardware.

Tools
We wrote the site as a single page in HTML, CSS and JavaScript. It uses the Poppins font and a dark space theme that matches our presentation. We built it with Claude as an AI assistant, designed our slides in Canva, hosted the site on GitHub Pages, and made a QR code for easy access. The images are NASA images, shown with credit lines, and many are artist's concepts.

Creativity
We treat missions as an investigation. The "case file" idea, the "mission ended, evidence remains" verdict, the afterlife timeline, and the detective-style quiz make space history feel like solving a mystery. Missions that aren't finished yet appear as "under construction".

What we considered

  • Accuracy: each mission links to NASA, and the pictures carry credits.
  • Accessibility: the layout works on phones, and the buttons and text are readable on dark backgrounds.
  • Speed: the pictures are resized so the page loads quickly.
  • Access: the site is public, with a QR code so judges can open it immediately.
  • Honesty: we credit NASA and state that this is an independent student project.
